title: Ezekiel 36:16–21
context: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel, reviewing why Israel went into exile. In their own land they defiled it by their ways and deeds, which the LORD compares to ritual uncleanness under the law (compare Leviticus 15:19); the image concerns impurity in worship, not a moral judgment on women. The LORD poured out wrath for bloodshed and idolatry and scattered them (36:18–19). Among the nations, their very presence as exiles caused the LORD’s holy name to be profaned, as people said, “These are the LORD’s people, and have left his land” (36:20). The LORD therefore had concern for his holy name (36:21). Both traditions read the unit as setting up the promise that follows: restoration will vindicate the LORD’s name before the nations.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel again. Arminian readers see a new movement in the chapter, turning from the land to the reasons for exile and the vindication of God’s name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as introducing a section grounded in divine authority. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the start of a review of Israel’s history that leads into the great promise of 36:22–32.

verses.text: “Son of man, when the house of Israel lived in their own land, they defiled it by their ways and by their deeds. Their way before me was as the uncleanness of a woman in her impurity.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Israel defiled the land by their ways, comparing it to ritual impurity under the law. Arminian readers see the image as stressing how deeply sin had affected worship and the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the comparison draws on ritual categories, compare Leviticus 15:19 by reference, to describe defilement before God. Both traditions read the image soberly as a picture of impurity, not as a judgment on women.

verses.text: Therefore I poured out my wrath on them for the blood which they had poured out on the land, and because they had defiled it with their idols.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD poured out wrath for the blood shed on the land and the idols that defiled it. Arminian readers see violence and idolatry as the two great sins that brought judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse naming the causes of judgment clearly, injustice toward people and unfaithfulness toward God. Shared ground: both traditions read the pairing as a reminder that true worship and justice belong together.

verses.text: I scattered them among the nations, and they were dispersed through the countries. I judged them according to their way and according to their deeds.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD scattered them among the nations, judging them according to their ways. Arminian readers see exile as the consequence of conduct, consistent with the earlier oracles of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s just sentence carried out in history. Both traditions read the verse as summarizing the exile as deserved judgment, the background against which the coming promise shines.

verses.text: When they came to the nations where they went, they profaned my holy name, in that men said of them, ‘These are the LORD’s people, and have left his land.’
verses.arminianNotes: Among the nations Israel profaned the LORD’s holy name, as people said, These are the LORD’s people, and have left his land. Arminian readers see how the exiles’ plight made God appear unable to keep his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the problem is named before the solution: the name has been profaned, and the LORD will act to address it. Shared ground: both traditions read the saying as showing that Israel’s exile reflected on the LORD’s reputation.

verses.text: But I had respect for my holy name, which the house of Israel had profaned among the nations where they went.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he had respect for his holy name, profaned among the nations. Arminian readers see God’s concern for his name as concern for the truth about himself being known by all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s commitment to his own glory as the ground of his action. Both traditions read the verse as the turning point: what follows flows from the LORD’s concern for his name.
